title: 論語 子張第十九
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 19, 〈子張〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 19 of the Analects, 子張 Zǐ zhāng, named, as every book is, from its first words — the disciple Zizhang, whose saying opens it. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 19 has 25 passages, and the Master speaks in none of them except at second hand: Zhu Xi says the whole book records the sayings of disciples, Zixia's the most and Zigong's next, since after Yan Hui none was quicker to understand than Zigong and after Master Zeng none more solid than Zixia. Zizhang opens with what makes an officer — ready to give his life in danger, thinking of what is right when gain is in sight — and with the man who holds virtue too narrowly to count either way (19.1–2); asked by Zixia's pupils about keeping company, he sets a broader rule against their teacher's (19.3). Zixia's sayings follow: small ways not to be followed far, learning day by day what one lacks, learning broadly and thinking of what is near, the craftsman in his workshop and the gentleman in his learning, the small man who dresses up his faults, the gentleman's three changes of aspect, winning trust before putting people to work or remonstrating, great virtue and small (19.4–11). Ziyou mocks Zixia's pupils as drilled in sweeping and answering but without the root, and Zixia answers that the Way is taught in order, as plants are told apart by kinds (19.12); then comes his pairing of office and learning (19.13). Ziyou and Master Zeng speak on mourning and on Zizhang, who aims too high (19.14–16); Master Zeng reports two sayings of the Master, on mourning for a parent and on Meng Zhuangzi, who kept his father's ministers and government (19.17–18), and tells a new officer of justice to pity the guilty, not to rejoice in finding them out (19.19). The last six passages are Zigong's: Zhou, the last Shang king, was not as wicked as his name, and that is why the gentleman will not live low down the stream, where all the world's bad things end up (19.20); the gentleman's faults are seen by all, like an eclipse, and so is his mending of them (19.21); the Master learned wherever the Way of the founding kings lived on among men (19.22); and to men who rated Zigong above the Master, or ran the Master down, he answers with a shoulder-high wall against one several times a man's height, hills against the sun and moon, and a Heaven no stair can climb (19.23–25). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子張曰：「
士見危致命，見得思義，
祭思敬，喪思哀，
其可已矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang said:
“An officer, seeing danger, hands over his life; seeing gain, he thinks of what is right;
at the sacrifice he thinks of reverence; in mourning he thinks of grief —
he will surely do, and that is all.”
sentences.i: Zizhang said: “An officer who will lay down his life in the face of danger, who thinks of what is right when there is gain in sight, who thinks of reverence when he sacrifices and of grief when he mourns — such a man will pass.”
sentences.n: The book is named 子張 from its opening words. Zhu Xi's heading: the whole book records the sayings of disciples, Zixia's the most and Zigong's next (此篇皆記弟子之言而子夏為多子貢次之); for after Yan Hui none in the school was quicker to understand than Zigong, and after Master Zeng none more solid than Zixia (盖孔門自顔子以下頴悟莫若子貢自曽子以下篤實無若子夏), so their words are recorded in detail. He counts twenty-five chapters (凡二十五章); our numbers are his. Zizhang is the disciple Zhuansun Shi 顓孫師 (2.18). 士 'an officer', a man of service (4.9, 13.20). 見 jiàn 'to see', twice. 致命 'to hand over one's life' — Zhu Xi: to give up one's life entirely, like saying 授命 (致命謂委致其命猶言授命也), the word of 14.13 見危授命 'seeing danger, he gives up his life'; Kong Anguo in He Yan: not to grudge one's own person (致命不愛其身也). 見得思義 'seeing gain, he thinks of what is right' is the last of the gentleman's nine thoughts at 16.10. 祭 jì 'to sacrifice'; 喪 sāng 'mourning'. Each clause is a situation followed by what the officer does in it, with the subject 士 left to carry over. 其可已矣: 其 'surely' softens the verdict, 可 'acceptable, will do', and 已矣 'and that is all'. Zhu Xi: these four are the great points on which a man's standing rests (四者立身之大節); fall short in one and nothing else about him is worth looking at (一有不至則餘無足觀), so Zizhang says an officer who can do these is nearly there (庶乎其可矣).

sentences.t:
子張曰：「
執德不𢎞，信道不篤，
焉能為有？焉能為亡？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang said:
“Holding to virtue, but not broadly; trusting the Way, but not firmly —
how can he count as having it? how can he count as lacking it?”
sentences.i: Zizhang said: “A man who keeps hold of virtue but in a narrow grip, and trusts the Way but without firmness — can you say he has them? Can you say he has not?”
sentences.n: 𢎞 is the edition's form of 弘 hóng 'broad' (8.7). 執 'to hold on to'; 篤 'firm, solid'. Each of the first two clauses sets a verb against a 不 that takes back half of it: he holds virtue, not broadly; he trusts the Way, not firmly. 焉 is yān 'how' (Zhu Xi: 焉於虔反), and 亡 is read as 無 wú 'not to have' (亡讀作無下同, 'and so below', at 19.5). 為 wéi 'to count as'. Zhu Xi: if a man keeps what he has gained too narrowly, his virtue stands alone (有所得而守之太狹則德孤); if he trusts what he has heard without firmness, the Way falls away (有所聞而信之不篤則道廢). 焉能為有，焉能為亡 is, he says, like saying 'not enough to make anything lighter or heavier' (猶言不足為輕重): whether such a man has them or not makes no difference. Kong Anguo in He Yan reads it the same way (言無所輕重也).

sentences.t:
子夏之門人問交於子張。
子張曰：「子夏云何？」
對曰：「子夏曰：『可者與之，其不可者拒之。』」
子張曰：「
異乎吾所聞：
君子尊賢而容衆，嘉善而矜不能。
我之大賢與，於人何所不容？
我之不賢與，人將拒我，如之何其拒人也？」

sentences.l:
Zixia's disciples asked Zizhang about dealing with others.
Zizhang said: “What does Zixia say?”
They answered: “Zixia says: ‘Those who are acceptable, keep company with; those who are not acceptable, turn away.’”
Zizhang said:
“That differs from what I have heard:
the gentleman honours the worthy and has room for the many; he praises the good and pities those who are not able.
Am I greatly worthy? Among others, whom would I not have room for?
Am I not worthy? Others will turn me away — how could I turn others away?”
sentences.i: Zixia's disciples asked Zizhang how one should deal with other people. “What does Zixia tell you?” said Zizhang. They answered: “Zixia says: ‘Keep company with those who are fit for it, and turn away those who are not.’” Zizhang said: “That is not what I was taught. A gentleman honours men of worth and makes room for everyone; he commends the good and feels for those who fall short. If I am a man of great worth, is there anyone I could not make room for? If I am not, others will turn me away — how would I come to be turning them away?”
sentences.n: 子夏 Zixia is the disciple Bu Shang 卜商 (1.7). 交 'dealing with others, association' — Kong Anguo in He Yan: they asked about the way of dealing with people (與人交接之道也). 云 'to say'. 可者 'those who are acceptable', 者 making a noun of 可; 與 yǔ 'to keep company with'. 拒 jù 'to turn away, to refuse'. 異乎 'differs from' (乎 = 於). 尊 'to honour'; 容 'to have room for, to tolerate'; 嘉 'to praise'; 矜 jīn 'to pity, to feel for'; 不能 'those who are not able'. In 我之大賢與, 之 between subject and predicate turns 'I am greatly worthy' into a phrase, and 與 yú puts it as a question (Zhu Xi: 賢與之與平聲): 'am I greatly worthy?' — each question then works as an 'if'. 如之何其拒人也 'how could it be that I turn others away?': 如之何 'how' (2.20), 其 'could (I)'. Zhu Xi: Zixia's words are cramped and narrow, and Zizhang is right to mock them (子夏之言廹狹子張譏之是也); but what Zizhang says has the fault of aiming too high (亦有過髙之弊): a man of great worth has room for all, yet must still break with grave wrongdoing (然大故亦所當絶); one not worthy may not turn people away, yet harmful friends (損友, 16.4) should still be kept at a distance (然損友亦所當逺); the learner must weigh this. Bao Xian in He Yan reconciles the two: in friendship one should go by Zixia, in general dealings by Zizhang (友交當如子夏汎交當如子張也). Variants: He Yan's text writes 距 for 拒 (the older loan form, the same word), reads 異乎吾所聞也 with a final 也, and 我大賢與, 我不賢與 without 之.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
雖小道，必有可觀者焉；
致逺恐泥，是以君子不為也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zixia said: “Even the small ways are sure to have something in them worth seeing. But take them far and you may well get mired, and that is why the gentleman does not take them up.”
sentences.n: 雖 'even, although'. 小道 'small ways' — Zhu Xi: things like farming and gardening, medicine and divination (小道如農圃醫卜之屬); He Yan's unsigned comment: other doctrines (小道謂異端也, the 異端 of 2.16). 可觀者 'something worth seeing', and 焉 yān 'in them' (the fused 於之). 致逺 'carried far'. 泥 is nì 'to get stuck' (Zhu Xi: 泥去聲…泥不通也, 'not getting through'; Bao Xian in He Yan: 泥難不通也). 是以 'this is why'. 為 wéi 'to practise, to take up'. Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: the hundred schools and the many skills are like ears, eyes, mouth and nose — each is clear in its own field but they cannot reach one another (百家衆技猶耳目口鼻皆有所明而不能相通); not that they have nothing worth seeing, but carried far they get stuck, and so the gentleman does not practise them.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
日知其所亡，月無忘其所能，
可謂好學也已矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zixia said:
“Each day knowing what he lacks, each month not forgetting what he can do —
he can be called fond of learning, and that is all.”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “Day by day to come to know what you still lack, month by month not to let slip what you can already do — that may truly be called fond of learning.”
sentences.n: 日 'each day' and 月 'each month' stand before their verbs as adverbs. 所 makes a noun of what follows: 其所亡 'what he lacks', 其所能 'what he can do'. 亡 is wú 'not to have' (Zhu Xi: 亡讀作無; 亡無也謂己之所未有, 'what one does not yet have'); Kong Anguo in He Yan takes it as what one has not yet heard of (日知其所未聞也). 好 hào 'fond of' (好去聲). 可謂好學也已矣 closes as 1.14 does (可謂好學也已), with a further 矣. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: one who is fond of learning renews himself daily and loses nothing (好學者日新而不失).

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
博學而篤志，切問而近思，
仁在其中矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zixia said:
“Learning broadly and setting one's aim firmly, asking earnestly and thinking of what is near at hand —
humaneness is there within it.”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “Study broadly and hold firmly to your aim; ask in earnest, and think about what is close at hand: humaneness lies right there within it.”
sentences.n: Four verbs, each with a word before it that says how, in two pairs joined by 而: 博學 'learning broadly' (6.25, 12.15), 篤志 'firmly setting one's aim', 切問 'asking earnestly' (切 qiè, as 切切 13.28), 近思 'thinking near'. 仁在其中矣 'humaneness is there within it', the shape of 2.18 and 15.31 (禄在其中矣). Zhu Xi: all four are matters of learning, asking, thinking and sifting, not yet the vigorous practice that makes humaneness (四者皆學問思辨之事耳未及乎力行而為仁也); but whoever works at them keeps his heart from racing outward, and what he holds ripens of itself — so 'humaneness is within it' (然從事於此則心不外馳而所存自熟故曰仁在其中矣). He quotes Master Cheng: thinking near means reasoning onward by kind (近思者以類而推); and a Mr Su: learning broadly with an aim not firm, one is large and achieves nothing; asking widely and thinking far, one toils without result (博學而志不篤則大而無成泛問逺思則勞而無功). Kong Anguo in He Yan glosses the first pair 愽學而厚識也 'to learn broadly and retain much', apparently taking 志 as 'to keep in mind'. He Yan's own unsigned comment: earnest asking is asking about what one has learned and not yet grasped, and near thinking is thinking about what one is able to reach (切問者切問於巳所學而未窹之事也近思者近思巳所能及之事也).

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
百工居肆以成其事，
君子學以致其道。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zixia said: “Craftsmen of every kind stay in their workshops to get their work done; the gentleman studies to carry his Way as far as it will go.”
sentences.n: 百工 'the hundred crafts', all the artisans. 肆 sì — Zhu Xi: the place in the government offices where things are made (肆謂官府造作之處). 以 'so as to', in both halves; the two halves are built alike, so the craftsman's workshop answers to the gentleman's learning. 致 'to carry to the utmost' (Zhu Xi: 致極也). Zhu Xi: a craftsman who does not stay in his workshop is drawn off to other things and his work is not refined (工不居肆則遷於異物而業不精); a gentleman who does not learn is carried off by outside lures and his aim is not firm (君子不學則奪於外誘而志不篤). He quotes Yin Tun: learning is the means of reaching the Way (學所以致其道也); craftsmen in their workshops must make it their business to finish their work — can the gentleman not know what his business is in learning? Zhu Xi judges that the two views need each other to make the sense complete (二説相須其義始備). Bao Xian in He Yan: as craftsmen in their workshops get their work done, so the gentleman learns to establish his Way (猶君子學以立其道也) — 致 read as 'to establish'.

sentences.t: 子夏曰：「小人之過也必文。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zixia said: “The small man's faults — he is sure to dress them up.”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “When a small man goes wrong, he will always paint it over.”
sentences.n: 小人之過也 'the small man's faults' is set up as the topic by 也 (as 人之過也, 4.7); 必文 'surely (he) glosses (them)'. 文 is a verb here, 'to give a fair surface to': Zhu Xi 文飾之也. He marks it 去聲 (wèn, the old reading of the verb); we print wén, as modern reading does — noted here once. Zhu Xi: the small man shrinks from correcting his fault but does not shrink from deceiving himself, so he must dress it up, and so doubles his fault (小人憚於改過而不憚於自欺故必文以重其過). Kong Anguo in He Yan: he dresses up his fault and does not tell the facts of it (文飾其過不言其情實也). The gentleman's faults come at 19.21.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
君子有三變：
望之儼然，
即之也溫，
聽其言也厲。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zixia said: “There are three changes in the gentleman. From a distance he has an air of dignity; close to, he is warm; and when you listen to what he says, he is exacting.”
sentences.n: 望 'to gaze at from a distance'; 即 'to go up to' (13.29, Zhu Xi 即就也). 也 marks each act as the topic: 'as for going up to him — warm'. 儼然 yǎn rán 'grave, dignified'. Zhu Xi: 儼然 is the dignity of his bearing, 溫 the mildness of his face, 厲 the sureness of his words (儼然者貌之莊溫者色之和厲者辭之確); Zheng Xuan in He Yan: 厲嚴正也 'severe and correct'. Compare 7.37 子温而厲 'the Master was gentle and yet grave'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: in other men, the dignified are not warm and the warm are not exacting; only Kongzi had all three (他人儼然則不溫溫則不厲惟孔子全之); and Xie Liangzuo: it is not that the gentleman means to change — the three go together without clashing (此非有意於變盖並行而不相悖也), like fine jade, warm and smooth yet firm (如良玉溫潤而栗然).

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
君子信而後勞其民；未信，則以為厲己也。
信而後諫；未信，則以為謗己也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zixia said:
“The gentleman is trusted, and only then works his people; not yet trusted, they take it as ill-using them.
He is trusted, and only then remonstrates; not yet trusted, (his lord) takes it as maligning him.”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “A gentleman must have the people's trust before he puts them to work; until he has it, they will think he means them harm. He must have his lord's trust before he remonstrates; until he has it, the lord will think he is speaking ill of him.”
sentences.n: 信 here is 'to be trusted' — Zhu Xi: true intent and heartfelt care, so that others trust him (信謂誠意惻怛而人信之也). 而後 'and only after that'. 勞 'to set to work'. 以為 'to take (it) as'. 厲 'to afflict, to ill-use' (Zhu Xi: 厲猶病也; Wang Su in He Yan: 厲病也); 謗 bàng 'to speak ill of, to malign'. 己 'oneself' refers back each time to whoever takes offence: the people in the first sentence, the lord in the second — neither is named. Zhu Xi: in serving those above and in directing those below, there must first be true intent and trust on both sides before anything can be done (事上使下皆必誠意交孚而後可以有為). Variant: He Yan's text ends 以爲謗巳矣 (巳 is that print's way of writing 己), with 矣 for the last 也.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
大德不踰閑，
小德出入可也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zixia said: “In the great points of conduct, never step over the bar; in the small ones, some going out and coming in is allowed.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: great virtue and small virtue are like saying great points and small points of conduct (大德小徳猶言大節小節). 閑 xián is a rail or barrier, the thing that stops things going out and in (閑闌也所以止物之出入) — so 出入 'going out and in' takes up the figure. 踰 'to overstep' (2.4 不踰矩). Zhu Xi: if a man first establishes the great, then even if his small points are not all in accord with principle, there is no harm (言人能先立乎其大者則小節雖或未盡合理亦無害也). He adds a Mr Wu's warning: the words of this chapter are not without their danger; let the learner look closely (此章之言不能無弊學者詳之). Kong Anguo in He Yan: 閑 is like 'the rule' (閑猶法也); small virtues cannot help overstepping the rule, so he says going out and in is allowable (小徳不能不踰法故曰出入可也).

sentences.t:
子游曰：「
子夏之門人小子，
當洒掃、應對、進退，則可矣。
抑末也；本之則無，如之何？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
You, in Ziyou's name (言偃, courtesy name 子游)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
what is to be done about it
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Ziyou said:
“Zixia's disciples, the young ones —
when it comes to sprinkling and sweeping, responding and answering, coming forward and withdrawing, they will do.
But these are branch-tips; trace them to the root, and there is nothing — what is to be done about it?”
sentences.i: Ziyou said: “Zixia's young disciples do well enough at sprinkling and sweeping the floor, answering when spoken to, and stepping forward and back. But that is only the tips of the branches. Of the root there is nothing at all — and what is to be done about that?”
sentences.n: 子游 Ziyou is the disciple Yan Yan 言偃 (2.7). 門人小子 'the disciples, the young ones'. 當 dāng 'facing, when it comes to'. 洒掃 'sprinkling (the floor with water) and sweeping': Zhu Xi spells 洒 色賣反 and 掃 素報反, which point to shài and sào; we give the modern sǎ sǎo, noted here once. 應對 'responding and answering' and 進退 'coming forward and withdrawing' are the forms a young man keeps before guests and elders. 則可矣 'then they will do'. 抑 'but' (14.33). 末 'the tip of a branch', against 本 'the root'; 本之 'to trace it to the root', 本 used as a verb with 之 its object. 如之何 'what is to be done about it?' (2.20). Zhu Xi: Ziyou is mocking Zixia's pupils: in dignified bearing and the measures of deportment they will do (於威儀容節之間則可矣), but this is only the branch-end of the Lesser Learning (然此小學之末耳); push back to its root — the setting right of the heart and making the intent true, as in the Great Learning (推其本如大學正心誠意之事) — and there is nothing. Bao Xian in He Yan: in receiving guests and attending to bearing and the forms of the rites they will do, but one cannot be without the root (不可無其本也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 抑未也 'but not yet', and Bao Xian's comment beside it has 人之未事 where the sense wants 末事 'branch matters' — probably the same confusion of 未 and 末 in that print.

sentences.t:
子夏聞之，曰：「
噫！言游過矣！
君子之道，孰先傳焉？孰後倦焉？
譬諸草木，區以别矣。
君子之道，焉可誣也？
有始有卒者，其惟聖人乎！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zixia heard of it and said:
“Hm! Yan You is wrong!
The gentleman's Way — which part is handed on first? which part is put off till later, wearied of?
Compare it to grasses and trees: they are told apart by kinds.
The gentleman's Way — how can it be made to deceive?
One who has the beginning and has the end — surely that is only the sage!”
sentences.i: Zixia heard of this and said: “Hm! Yan You is wrong. In the gentleman's Way, which part is handed on first, and which is put off till later as though one had tired of teaching it? Think of grasses and trees: they are sorted by kind. How could anyone teach the gentleman's Way so as to mislead the learner? To have both the beginning and the end in hand — surely only a sage can do that!”
sentences.n: 噫 yī, a cry of displeasure, 'hm!' as at 13.20 (Kong Anguo in He Yan: 噫心不平之聲也; Zhu Xi's gloss at 13.20 is much the same). 言游 Yan You: Zixia calls Ziyou by his surname and courtesy name. 過 'to be wrong, to go too far'. 傳 chuán 'to hand on (a teaching)'. 倦 'to weary of', as in 誨人不倦 'to teach others and never weary of it' (7.2; Zhu Xi: 倦如誨人不倦之倦). The two 焉 that end the questions are yān as a final particle; 焉可誣也 has yān 'how' (Zhu Xi: 焉於虔反). 譬諸 'compare it to' (諸 = 之於). 區 qū 'kind, class' (Zhu Xi: 區猶類也); 别 bié 'to tell apart' (Zhu Xi: 别必列反). Zhu Xi on the whole: the gentleman's Way does not hand on the branch first because it comes first, nor put the root last because he is tired of teaching it; it is only that learners reach different depths, as grasses and trees differ in size and are of different kinds. To force the high and far on them without measuring how deep they have gone or how ripe they are is to deceive them (則是誣之而已); how could the gentleman's Way be like that? To string beginning and end, root and branch on one thread (若夫始終本末一以貫之, cf. 4.15) belongs to the sage alone — how could one demand it of young disciples (豈可責之門人小子乎)? 卒 zú 'the end'. 其惟…乎 'surely only…!'. He quotes Master Cheng: the gentleman teaches in order, handing on first what is small and near and afterwards teaching what is great and far — not that after the near and small he never teaches the far and great (非先傳以近小而後不教以逺大也); and, sprinkling and sweeping, responding and answering are themselves what lies above form (洒掃應對便是形而上者), since principle has no great or small. Zhu Xi's judgment (愚按): the learner should go in order and advance by degrees, not despise the branch and seek the root (學者當循序而漸進不可厭末而求本). The older readings differ. Bao Xian in He Yan: whoever hands on the great work first is sure to tire of it (先傳大業者必猒倦), so Zixia teaches his pupils small things first and the great Way later. Ma Rong: the great Way and the small differ like grasses and trees of different kinds — learning must go in order (言學當以次也); and he takes 誣 as 'to misrepresent': how can anyone be allowed to misrepresent the gentleman's Way by saying my pupils can only sprinkle and sweep? Kong Anguo: only the sage is the same from end to beginning (終始如一唯聖人耳也).

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
仕而優則學，
學而優則仕。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zixia said: “When office leaves you strength to spare, study; when study leaves you strength to spare, take office.”
sentences.n: 優 yōu 'ample, with something over' (14.12): Zhu Xi 優有餘力也 'having strength to spare'. 而 joins the state to the condition, and 則 'then' gives what follows; the second line turns the first around. Zhu Xi: office and learning share one principle but are different affairs, so whoever is at one must first do it fully before he can reach the other (仕與學理同而事異故當其事者必先有以盡其事而後可及其餘); but learning while in office deepens what serves the office, and taking office while learning widens the testing of the learning (仕而學則所以資其仕者益深學而仕則所以驗其學者益廣). Ma Rong in He Yan: if in what one does one has strength to spare, use it to learn letters (行有餘力則以學文也) — the words of 1.6.

sentences.t: 子游曰：「喪致乎哀而止。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
You, in Ziyou's name (言偃, courtesy name 子游)

sentences.l: Ziyou said: “Mourning goes to the utmost of grief, and stops there.”
sentences.i: Ziyou said: “In mourning, let grief run its full course — and there stop.”
sentences.n: 喪 sāng 'mourning'. 致 'to carry to the utmost', and 乎 here is 'in, of' (= 於): 致乎哀 'reach the utmost in grief'. 而止 'and stop'. Zhu Xi: carry grief to its utmost, without prizing ornament (致極其哀不尚文飾也); he quotes Yang Shi: it has the sense of 'with mourning, rather than smoothly ordered, better grieving' (喪與其易也寧戚, 3.4) — better the rites fall short and grief be more than enough (不若禮不足而哀有餘之意). But in his own judgment (愚按) the two words 而止 have a slight fault of aiming high and far and passing over fine detail (而止二字亦微有過於髙逺而簡畧細微之弊); let the learner look closely. Kong Anguo in He Yan reads 而止 as a limit: one may waste away in grief but not harm one's life (毀不傷性也).

sentences.t:
子游曰：「
吾友張也，為難能也，
然而未仁。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
You, in Ziyou's name (言偃, courtesy name 子游)

sentences.i: Ziyou said: “My friend Zhang can manage what others find hard to manage; but he is not yet humane.”
sentences.n: 張 Zhang is Zizhang, called by the 張 of his courtesy name, without the 子, as a friend would. 也 sets him up as the topic. 為難能 'does what is hard to be able (to do)': 難 nán 'hard', 能 'to be able'. 然而 'so it is, and yet' — 'but'. 未仁 'not yet humane'. Zhu Xi: Zizhang's conduct aimed too high, and he was short of true, heartfelt care (子張行過髙而少試實惻怛之意; the edition's 試 is most likely a slip for 誠 'true'); compare 11.15 師也過 'Shi goes past'. Bao Xian in He Yan takes the praise to be of his bearing: Zizhang's manner and deportment were hard to match (言子張容儀之難及也).

sentences.t:
曽子曰：「
堂堂乎張也，
難與並為仁矣。」

morph.gloss: the edition's form of 曾, in the name 曽子 (14.28)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said:
“Imposing, how imposing Zhang is!
It is hard to practise humaneness side by side with him.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “What a fine figure Zhang cuts! But it is hard to work at humaneness alongside him.”
sentences.n: 曽 is the edition's form of 曾: Master Zeng is Zeng Shen 曾參 (1.4). 堂堂 táng táng 'imposing' — Zhu Xi: the fullness of his looks and bearing (堂堂容貌之盛). The predicate comes first and 乎 makes it an exclamation; 也 closes the subject: 'imposing — Zhang!' 難與並為仁 'hard with (him) side by side to practise humaneness': 與 yǔ 'with', 並 bìng 'side by side', 為仁 'to practise humaneness' (1.2). Zhu Xi: he worked at the outside and set himself high (言其務外自髙), so one could not help him to humaneness, nor could he help others in theirs (不可輔而為仁亦不能有以輔人之仁也). He quotes Fan Zuyu: Zizhang had more than enough outside and not enough within, so none of the disciples would grant that he was humane (子張外有餘而内不足故門人皆不與其為仁); the Master said 'firm, resolute, plain, slow of speech — near to humaneness' (剛毅木訥近仁, 13.27). Zheng Xuan in He Yan: Zizhang's bearing was imposing, but in the Way of humaneness he was thin (於仁道薄也).

sentences.t:
曽子曰：「
吾聞諸夫子：
人未有自致者也，
必也親喪乎！」

morph.gloss: the edition's form of 曾, in the name 曽子 (14.28)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said:
“I heard it from the Master:
among people none yet has of himself gone to the utmost;
if it must be, surely at a parent's mourning!”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “I have heard the Master say that there is nothing in which a man spends himself to the very utmost of his own accord — unless it is the mourning for a parent.”
sentences.n: 聞諸夫子 'heard it from the Master' (諸 = 之於). 人未有自致者也 'among people there has not yet been one who of himself goes to the utmost': 者 makes 'one who…' of 自致. 致 — Zhu Xi: to go to the very limit (致盡其極也); this is where a man's true feeling cannot stop itself (盖人之真情所不能自已者). 必也…乎 'if it must be (something), surely…' (as 3.7, 12.13, 13.3). 親 'parents'; 喪 sāng 'mourning'. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: mourning for one's parents is surely where one gives oneself wholly; if one does not use one's sincerity here, where will one use it (親喪固所自盡也於此不用其誠惡乎用其誠)? Ma Rong in He Yan: though people cannot give themselves fully in other things, at the mourning of their parents they are sure to (至於親䘮必自致盡也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 人未有自致也者, with 也者 for 者也.

sentences.t:
曽子曰：「
吾聞諸夫子：
孟莊子之孝也，其他可能也；
其不改父之臣與父之政，是難能也。」

morph.gloss: the edition's form of 曾, in the name 曽子 (14.28)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Meng Zhuangzi — a grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said:
“I heard it from the Master:
Meng Zhuangzi's filial devotion — the other parts of it can be managed;
his not changing his father's ministers and his father's government — this is hard to manage.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “I have heard the Master say: in Meng Zhuangzi's devotion as a son, the rest is within others' reach; but that he made no change to his father's ministers or to his father's government — that is hard to match.”
sentences.n: 孟莊子 Meng Zhuangzi — Zhu Xi: a grandee of Lu named Su; his father Xianzi was named Mie (孟莊子魯大夫名速其父獻子名蔑); Ma Rong in He Yan: Zhongsun Su (仲孫速). 孝 'filial devotion'. 其他可能也 'its other (parts) can be managed' — by others as well. 其不改… 'his not changing…' is the subject, taken up again by 是 'this'; 與 yǔ 'and'; 難能 'hard to manage'. Zhu Xi: Xianzi had worthy virtue, and Zhuangzi was able to employ his ministers and keep up his government (獻子有賢德而莊子能用其臣守其政); so his other filial acts, though praiseworthy, were none of them as hard as this (故其他孝行雖有可稱而皆不若此事之為難). Compare 1.11 and 4.20, 'three years without changing from his father's way'. Ma Rong places it during the mourning seclusion (謂在諒闇之中; the 諒隂 of 14.43): even what was not good he could not bear to change (雖不善者不忍改也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 是難也 'this is hard', without 能.

sentences.t:
孟氏使陽膚為士師，問於曽子。
曽子曰：「
上失其道，民散久矣。
如得其情，則哀矜而勿喜。」

morph.gloss: the Meng — the Mengsun house of Lu
Yang Fu — a disciple of Master Zeng
an officer, a man of service
the edition's form of 曾, in the name 曽子 (14.28)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the edition's form of 曾, in the name 曽子 (14.28)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Meng made Yang Fu officer of justice; he asked Master Zeng.
Master Zeng said:
“Those above have lost their Way; the people have long been scattered.
If you get at the true facts, then grieve and pity, and do not rejoice.”
sentences.i: When the Meng house made Yang Fu officer of justice, he went to Master Zeng for counsel. Master Zeng said: “Those above have lost the Way, and the people have long since drifted apart. When you do get to the truth of a case, be sorry for them and pity them; take no pleasure in it.”
sentences.n: 孟氏 the Meng are the Mengsun house of Lu (孟孫, 2.5; 18.3). 陽膚 Yang Fu — Zhu Xi and Bao Xian in He Yan: a disciple of Master Zeng (陽膚曽子弟子). 使 shǐ 'to make (someone do)'; 為 wéi 'to serve as'. 士師 'officer of justice', over trials and prisons (18.2; Bao Xian: 士師典獄官也). 問 'to ask' — what he asked is left unsaid; the answer shows it was how to do the work. 散 sàn 'to scatter' — Zhu Xi: the bonds of feeling and right have come apart and no longer hold the people together (民散謂情義乖離不相維繫). 久矣 'long since'. 如 'if'; 其情 'their true state', the facts of a case. 哀矜 'to grieve and pity' (矜 jīn, as 19.3); 勿 'do not'. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: the people scatter because they were used without the Way and taught without constancy (民之散也以使之無道教之無素); so when they break the law, either they were driven by what they could not help or they fell into it unknowing (非迫於不得已則陷於不知也) — and so, when you get the facts, grieve and do not rejoice. Ma Rong in He Yan: the people's scattering, their drifting and lawbreaking, is the doing of those above and not the people's fault (乃上之所為也非民之過也); you should pity them, and not be pleased with yourself for getting the facts.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
紂之不善，
不如是之甚也。
是以君子惡居下流，
天下之惡皆歸焉。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Zhou — last king of the Shang
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said:
“Zhou's not being good —
it was not so extreme as this.
This is why the gentleman hates to dwell low down the stream:
the bad things of all under Heaven all end up in it.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “Zhou's wickedness was never as extreme as it is now made out to be. That is why a gentleman hates to settle in the low ground at the bottom of the stream: everything bad in the world comes draining down into it.”
sentences.n: 紂 Zhou is the last king of the Shang, the man behind the 之 'him' of 18.1. 之 between subject and verb makes 紂不善 'Zhou was not good' into one phrase, 'Zhou's not being good', the topic; 不如是之甚 'was not like this extremity', not as bad as this — as bad as the name he now has. 是以 'by this, this is why', as at 5.14. 惡 is wù 'to hate' in 惡居 (Zhu Xi: 惡居之惡去聲) and è 'the bad' in 天下之惡, which has no mark and is read as written. 下流 'the lower stream' (as 17.24): Zhu Xi — the lie of the land where it is low, where many streams come together (下流地形卑下之處衆流之所歸), a figure for a man who has some real taint of filth and meanness and then becomes the place where bad names gather too (喻人身有汙賤之實亦惡名之所聚也). 歸 'to go back to, to end up in'; 焉 yān 'in it' (the fused 於之). Zhu Xi: Zigong says this so that men will always watch themselves and never once set themselves in a place of wrong (子貢言此欲人常自警省不可一置其身於不善之地); it does not mean that Zhou was really guiltless and bore a bad name for nothing (非謂紂本無罪而虚被惡名也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: later ages hated him extremely and laid the world's evils at his door (後丗憎甚之皆以天下之悪歸之於紂也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 紂之不善也, with 也 after the topic; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
君子之過也，
如日月之食焉：
過也，人皆見之；
更也，人皆仰之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said:
“The gentleman's faults —
they are like the sun and moon being eclipsed:
when he errs, people all see it;
when he changes, people all look up at him.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “When a gentleman goes wrong, it is like the sun or the moon going dark: while the fault is there everyone can see it, and once he has put it right, people all raise their eyes to him again.”
sentences.n: 之 makes 君子過 'the gentleman errs' into a phrase, 'the gentleman's faults', and 也 holds it up as the topic. 食 shí 'to eat' is also the word for an eclipse, the sun or moon being 'eaten'; He Yan's text writes it 蝕. 之 again turns 日月食 'sun and moon are eclipsed' into a phrase. 焉 here only closes the sentence. 過也…更也… : each verb with 也 after it sets up a condition, 'erring — …; changing — …'. 更 is gēng 'to change, to correct' (Zhu Xi: 更平聲, the level tone; Kong Anguo in He Yan: 更改也). 仰 'to look up at' (9.10). Zhu Xi gives this chapter nothing but the sound mark. Nothing is hidden either way: the fault is seen by everyone, and so is the mending. Variant: He Yan's text reads 如日月之蝕也, with 蝕 for 食 and 也 for the final 焉.

sentences.t: 衞公孫朝問於子貢曰：「仲尼焉學？」

morph.gloss: Gongsun Chao — a grandee of Wei
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Gongsun Chao of Wei asked of Zigong, saying: “Where did Zhongni learn?”
sentences.i: Gongsun Chao of Wei asked Zigong: “Where did Zhongni learn what he knows?”
sentences.n: 衞 is the edition's form of 衛, the state of Wei (7.14). 公孫朝 Gongsun Chao — Zhu Xi: a grandee of Wei (公孫朝衞大夫), as Ma Rong in He Yan (朝衞大夫也); 朝 is read cháo (Zhu Xi: 朝音潮). 仲尼 Zhongni is Kongzi, named by his courtesy name, as the speakers of 19.22–19.25 name him, Zigong among them; Zhu Xi, explaining 19.24, puts 孔子 in his place (自絶於孔子). 焉 is yān 'where?' (Zhu Xi: 焉於䖍反), put before the verb as question words are: 焉學 'where learn?' — from whom had he learned what he knew?

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
文武之道，未墜於地，在人。
賢者識其大者，
不賢者識其小者，
莫不有文武之道焉。
夫子焉不學？
而亦何常師之有？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said:
“The Way of Wen and Wu has not fallen to the ground; it is among men.
Those who are worthy remember its great parts;
those not worthy remember its small parts;
there is no one who does not have the Way of Wen and Wu in him.
Where did the Master not learn?
And besides, what constant teacher did he have?”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “The Way of King Wen and King Wu has not dropped into the dust; it lives on in people. The worthy keep hold of the large things in it, the less worthy of the small, and there is no one without some share of it. Is there anywhere our Master did not learn? And what one fixed teacher did he ever have?”
sentences.n: 文 and 武 are King Wen and King Wu, the founders of the Zhou (9.5, 8.20), each named by his title alone. Zhu Xi: the Way of Wen and Wu means their counsels and instructions and their achievements, together with all the rites, music and ordered forms of the Zhou (文武之道謂文王武王之謨訓功烈與凡周之禮樂文章皆是也). 墜 zhuì 'to fall'. 在人 'it is in men': Zhu Xi — there are men who can keep it in memory (在人言人有能記之者). 識 is zhì 'to remember, to keep in mind', both times (Zhu Xi: 識音志…識記也). 其大者 'its great ones', its larger parts: 者 makes 大 and 小 into things. 莫不有…焉 'there is no one who does not have … in him': 焉 is the fused 於之. The 焉 of 夫子焉不學 is yān 'where?' (Zhu Xi: 下焉字於䖍反, marking this second one): 'where did the Master not learn?' — nowhere. 何常師之有 'what constant teacher did he have?': the object 何常師 is put before the verb and marked by 之. Kong Anguo in He Yan: worthy and unworthy each had something they remembered, and there was no one the Master did not learn from (夫子無所不從學也), so he had no constant teacher (無所不從學故無常師也). Compare the Master's own words at 7.21: among three men walking there is sure to be a teacher for him.

sentences.t: 叔孫武叔語大夫於朝曰：「子貢賢於仲尼。」

words.reading: 叔孫武叔 shū sūn wǔ shū

morph.gloss: Shusun Wushu — a grandee of Lu
grandson (with 叔, the clan name Shusun)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l: Shusun Wushu told the grandees at court: “Zigong is worthier than Zhongni.”
sentences.i: Shusun Wushu remarked to the grandees at court: “Zigong is a better man than Zhongni.”
sentences.n: 叔孫武叔 Shusun Wushu — Zhu Xi: a grandee of Lu named Zhouchou (武叔魯大夫名州仇); Ma Rong in He Yan: Shusun Zhouchou, 武 Wu being his posthumous name (鲁大夫叔孫州仇也武謚也). The Shusun were one of the Three Families of Lu (3.2). 語 is yù 'to tell, to speak to' (Zhu Xi: 語去聲), and 朝 cháo 'the court' (朝音潮). 賢於 'worthier than': 於 after a quality word marks the comparison.

sentences.t:
子服景伯以告子貢。
子貢曰：「
譬之宮牆：
賜之牆也及肩，
窺見室家之好。」

words.reading: 子服景伯 zǐ fú jǐng bó

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to submit, to be won over
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zifu Jingbo reported it to Zigong.
Zigong said:
“Liken it to the walls of a dwelling:
Ci's wall reaches the shoulder;
peeping over, one sees the fine things of rooms and household.”
sentences.i: Zifu Jingbo passed the remark on to Zigong. Zigong said: “Take the walls about a dwelling. My wall stands shoulder-high: peep over it, and all that is good in house and household is in view.”
sentences.n: 子服景伯 Zifu Jingbo is the grandee of Lu of 14.38, where too he reports (以告) what a man has said; 以 'with it', the thing reported left unsaid. 譬之 'liken it': 之 is the matter in hand, Zigong's worth against the Master's. 宮 gōng is a dwelling, any house, and 牆 its wall. 賜 Ci is Zigong's personal name: he names himself, as at 5.8. 也 after 賜之牆 holds it up as the topic. 及肩 'reaches the shoulder'. 窺 kuī 'to peep, to look over' (Ruan's text writes 闚, the same word); 見 jiàn 'to see'. 室家之好 'the fine things of rooms and household': 好 is hǎo 'good, fine' (no mark). Zhu Xi: the wall low, the rooms shallow (牆卑室淺) — all there is can be seen from outside. Zigong's words run on past Zhu Xi's comments through units 26–27, which stand unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 譬諸宮牆也, 諸 'it to' for 之, with a final 也; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
夫子之牆數仞，
不得其門而入，
不見宗廟之美，
百官之富。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to take as chief, to look up to as head (Zhu Xi: 主)

sentences.i: Our Master's wall rises several times a man's height. Unless you find the gate and go in, you never see the splendour of the ancestral temple or the riches of its hundred offices.
sentences.n: Zigong is still speaking: the words run on from unit 25, past Zhu Xi's comment, and stand unquoted. 夫子 here is the Master. 數 is shù 'several' (as 7.16 數年). 仞 rèn is a length of seven feet (Zhu Xi: 七尺曰仞; Bao Xian in He Yan: 七尺曰仞也). 不得其門而入 'not finding its gate and going in' is the condition, and 不見… 'one does not see…' what follows from it. 宗廟 'the ancestral temple' (11.25, 14.20). 百官 'the hundred offices', as at 14.43. 富 'wealth, richness'. Zhu Xi: if one does not go in by its gate one does not see what is inside; it says the wall is high and the house broad (七尺曰仞不入其門則不見其中之所有言牆髙而宫廣也). Variants: He Yan's text reads 夫子之牆也數仞, with 也 after the topic, and 不得其門而入者 'those who do not find its gate and go in'.

sentences.t:
得其門者或寡矣。
夫子之云，不亦宜乎？

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Those who find its gate are perhaps few.
That lord's saying so — is it not fitting indeed?
sentences.i: And those who find the gate may well be few. Little wonder, then, that his lordship talks as he does.
sentences.n: Still Zigong, unquoted, continuing unit 25. 得其門者 'those who find its gate'; 或 'perhaps, it may be'; 寡 'few'. 夫子 is not the Master here but Shusun Wushu, 'that lord' (Zhu Xi: 此夫子指武叔; Bao Xian in He Yan: 夫子謂武叔也), as 夫子 is Jisun at 14.38. 之 makes 夫子云 'that lord says (so)' into a phrase; 云 'to say'. 不亦宜乎 'is it not fitting indeed?' — the frame of 1.1 不亦說乎. Few find the gate, and Wushu, it is implied, is not one of them.

sentences.t:
叔孫武叔毁仲尼。
子貢曰：「
無以為也！
仲尼不可毁也。
他人之賢者，丘陵也，
猶可踰也；
仲尼，日月也，
無得而踰焉。
人雖欲自絶，
其何傷於日月乎？
多見其不知量也。」

words.reading: 叔孫武叔 shū sūn wǔ shū

morph.gloss: Sun, 'grandson', the clan name's last part (孟孫, 季孫, 仲孫)
Wu, posthumous name of Meng Wubo
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
Shusun Wushu disparaged Zhongni.
Zigong said:
“There is no use doing this!
Zhongni cannot be disparaged.
Other men's worthy ones are hills and mounds:
they can still be got over;
Zhongni is the sun and moon:
there is no managing to get over them.
Though a man may wish to cut himself off,
what harm would that do to the sun and moon?
Only his not knowing his measure would be seen.”
sentences.i: Shusun Wushu ran down Zhongni. Zigong said: “Save yourself the trouble — Zhongni is beyond running down. The worth of other men is a hill or a ridge, and one can still climb past it; Zhongni is the sun and the moon, and there is no climbing past those. A man may choose to turn his back on them, but what does that take from the sun and moon? It only lets everyone see how little he knows his own size.”
sentences.n: 毁 'to disparage, to run down' (15.24). 無以為也 'there is nothing to do it by', 'it is no use' — Zhu Xi: like saying there is no use doing this (無以為猶言無用為此). 他人之賢者 'the worthy ones among other men'. 丘 qiū and 陵 líng — Zhu Xi: earth piled high is a 丘, a great mound a 陵 (土高曰丘大阜曰陵); the sun and moon stand for the Master's utmost height (日月喻其至高). 猶 'still'; 踰 'to cross over, to get past'. 無得而踰焉 'there is no managing to get over them': 得 'to manage to', and 焉 at the end stands where 之 'them' would, the object of 踰. 自絶 'to cut oneself off' — Zhu Xi: to cut oneself off from Kongzi by slander (自絶謂以謗毁自絶於孔子). 其何傷於日月乎 'what harm would it do to the sun and moon?': 其 makes the question rhetorical. 多 is not 'much' here: Zhu Xi says it is the same as 祇 'only' and glosses it 'just' (多與祇同適也); the pinyin stays duō. 見 jiàn 'to be seen' (no mark). 量 is liàng 'measure, capacity' (Zhu Xi: 量去聲): not knowing one's measure is not knowing one's own portion and measure (不知量謂不自知其分量). He Yan's unsigned comment: though a man wishes to cut himself off from the sun and moon, how can he harm them? it just shows of itself that he does not know his measure (言人雖自欲絶棄於日月其何能傷之乎適自見不知量). Variants: He Yan's text reads 仲尼如日月也 'Zhongni is like the sun and moon', adding 如, and 人雖欲自絶也, with a final 也.

sentences.t:
陳子禽謂子貢曰：「
子為恭也，
仲尼豈賢於子乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.i: Chen Ziqin said to Zigong: “This is your deference talking, sir. How could Zhongni be a better man than you?”
sentences.n: 陳子禽 Chen Ziqin is Ziqin 子禽 of 1.10, called Chen Kang 陳亢 at 16.13; 陳 is the surname. 謂…曰 'said to … saying'. 子 'you, sir'. 為恭 wéi gōng 'to be respectful, to show respect': Zhu Xi — showing respect and giving way to his teacher (為恭謂為恭敬推遜其師也). 豈 qǐ makes the question rhetorical, 'how could…?'. 賢於子 'worthier than you'. It is Shusun Wushu's comparison (19.23), put now to Zigong's face.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
君子一言以為知，
一言以為不知，
言不可不慎也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said:
“The gentleman by one word is counted wise,
by one word is counted not wise;
with words one cannot but be careful.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “A single remark can earn a gentleman the name of wise, and a single remark can lose it. Words have to be weighed before they are spoken.”
sentences.n: Zigong rebukes him before he answers — Zhu Xi: he reproves Ziqin for not being careful in speech (責子禽不謹言). 一言以為知 'by one word (he) is counted wise': 以 'by it' points back to 一言, and 為 wéi is 'to be counted as'. 知 is zhì 'wise' both times (Zhu Xi: 知去聲). 言不可不慎 'words cannot not be careful': the double negative makes a strong 'must'. Zigong's answer runs on past Zhu Xi's comments through units 31–32, which stand unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text writes 智 'wise' for 知, both times — the graph later used for this word.

sentences.t:
夫子之不可及也，
猶天之不可階而升也。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master's not being reachable
is like Heaven's not being climbable by steps.
sentences.i: No one can come up to our Master, any more than a man could set a stair against the sky and climb into it.
sentences.n: Still Zigong, unquoted, continuing his answer of unit 30. 之 in both halves turns a clause into a phrase: 'the Master's not being reachable' is like 'Heaven's not being climbable'. 及 'to reach, to come up to' (5.20). 階 jiē, a flight of steps (10.4), is used as a verb, 'to go up by steps' — Zhu Xi: 階梯也, a stair. 升 'to go up'. Zhu Xi on why it cannot be done: greatness can be achieved, but transforming cannot (大可為也化不可為也), and so it says not to be climbed by steps. Variant: He Yan's text has no 也 after 夫子之不可及.

sentences.t:
夫子之得邦家者，
所謂立之斯立，
道之斯行，
綏之斯來，
動之斯和，
其生也榮，
其死也哀，
如之何其可及也？

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to

sentences.i: Had our Master ever come to hold a state or a great house, it would have been just as the saying has it: he sets them on their feet and they stand, he leads them and they go along, he gives them ease and they come to him, he stirs them and they are of one accord. Living, he would be held in honour; dead, he would be mourned. How could anyone come up to him?
sentences.n: Still Zigong, unquoted, ending the answer begun in unit 30. 夫子之得邦家者 'the Master's getting a state or a house': 之 makes it a phrase, and 者 sets it up as a supposition — he never did. Kong Anguo in He Yan: it means becoming a lord of a state or a minister or grandee (謂爲諸侯若卿大夫也); 邦 and 家 as at 17.18. 所謂 'what is called' brings in words that sound like a known saying. Four pairs follow, each 'do X to them, then (斯) they Y'. Zhu Xi glosses each: 立之 'setting them up' means establishing their livelihood (立之謂植其生也); 道 is dǎo 'to lead' (= 導; Zhu Xi: 道去聲…道引也謂教之也, 'it means teaching them'), and 行 'they follow' (行從也); 綏 suí 'to give ease' (綏安也), and 來 'they come and attach themselves' (來歸附也); 動 'to rouse', to drum and dance them on (動謂鼓舞之也), and 和 is the concord of the people 'changed, and so at peace', in a phrase he cites (和所謂於變時雍). So wonderful and quick is the answer they make him (言其感應之妙神速如此). 其生也榮 'his living — glory': none would fail to honour and love him (榮謂莫不尊親); 其死也哀 'his dying — grief': they would mourn as for a dead father and mother (哀則如喪考妣). 榮 róng. 如之何 'how?' (2.20), with 其 'could he'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: this is the sage's spirit-like transforming, flowing on with Heaven and Earth above and below (此聖人之神化上下與天地同流者也); and Xie Liangzuo: from Zigong's words on the sage one knows how far his own virtue had advanced in his later years (觀子貢稱聖人語乃知晚年進德盖極於高逺也). Kong Anguo in He Yan reads the pairs the same way: give them ease and those far off come (安之則逺者来至), rouse them and none is not in concord (動之則莫不和穆也), so that in life he is honoured and in death mourned (生則見榮顯死則見哀痛). Variants: He Yan's text writes 導 'to lead' for 道, the graph of the reading dǎo, and reads 夫子得邦家者 without 之.
